items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a marine-exhibit model-ship cradle beam of total length L = 2.8 m and mass 26 kg hangs horizontally in equilibrium from two light vertical ceiling wires attached at A and B, separated by 1.8 m. Its centre of gravity G lies 1.15 m to the right of attachment A and 0.65 m to the left of attachment B (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B yield T₁ = 92.11 N ≈ 92.1 N. (b) Force balance gives T₂ = 163.0 N ≈ 163 N. (c) wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.

markScheme.criterion: Applies moment balance about attachment B.
Applies ΣF_y = 0 to obtain T₂.
Identifies the wire closer to G as carrying greater tension.
Justifies using equal opposite moments about G with shorter lever arm.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about attachment B, calculate the tension T₁ in wire A.
workingSteps: Since wire A is vertical, T₁ = 92.11 N ≈ 92.1 N.

parts.prompt: Using vertical force equilibrium, determine the tension T₂ in wire B.
State which wire carries the greater tension and justify your answer qualitatively in terms of moments about the centre of gravity.
parts.expectedAnswer: In equilibrium, wire B carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire B.
workingSteps: Take moments about the centre of gravity so the weight has zero moment.
Show that the wire with the shorter perpendicular distance to G must exert the larger tension to balance moments.

items.stem: Two equal and opposite parallel forces, each of magnitude F = 134 N, are applied to the ends of a wind-tunnel pitch-adjuster crossbar of length d = 0.56 m, each inclined at 50° to the bar, as illustrated in the diagram.
items.workedSolution: (a) Static equilibrium requires zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point. (b) Torque of the couple is T = F d_perp = 57.48 N m ≈ 57.5 N m (note N m, not J).

markScheme.criterion: Zero resultant force.
Zero resultant moment about any point.
Applies T = F d_perp using perpendicular separation.
Torque = 57.5 N m with unit N m.

parts.prompt: State the two conditions necessary for a rigid body to be in static equilibrium.
parts.expectedAnswer: The body must satisfy zero resultant force and zero resultant moment about any point.
workingSteps: State zero resultant force for translational equilibrium.
State zero resultant moment about any point for rotational equilibrium.

items.stem: Weighing 240 N, a modular shelter unit slides at constant velocity down a straight unloading track, covering a distance of 20 m along the slope for a vertical drop of 4.8 m.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p = W h (not W L).
Obtains 1.15 × 10³ J.
Uses constant speed (ΔE_k = 0) so F_res L = ΔE_p.
Obtains 57.6 N.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a university courtyard banner boom is a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 1.4 m and mass 12 kg smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 4 kg hangs so that its centre of gravity acts 1.2 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at an angle of 54° above the horizontal rod (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the horizontal component of force exerted on the rod by hinge O?
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 54° × 1.4 = (12 × 0.7 + 4 × 1.2) × 9.81 = 129.5 N m. Hence T sin 54° = 92.49 N and T = 114.3 N ≈ 114 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 54° = 67.20 N ≈ 67.2 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (12 + 4) × 9.81 − 92.49 = 64.47 N ≈ 64.5 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 67.2 N.

items.stem: In Searle's Young modulus investigation (RP4) on a annealed copper wire of unstretched length $(2.10 \pm 0.002)$ m, micrometer diameter measurements at three orthogonal positions average to 0.48 mm, 0.46 mm, and 0.47 mm (each $\pm 0.01$ mm). Plotting load $F$ against extension $e$ yields a straight line through the origin of gradient 9.8 N mm⁻¹ ($\pm 1.8\%$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.73 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. (b) $E = L(\mathrm{grad})/A = 119 GPa$. (c) $\%\Delta E = 6.15%$. (d) an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while orthogonal micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Averages three diameters and converts mm to m in $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 1.73 × 10⁻⁷ m²$.
Converts gradient to N m⁻¹ and substitutes into $E = (L/A)\,\mathrm{grad}$.
Young modulus $E = 119 GPa$.
Combines $\%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad}$.
Percentage uncertainty in $E = 6.15%$.
Identical reference wire compensates both support sag and temperature expansion.
Orthogonal micrometer readings at >= 3 positions detect non-uniformity/oval cross-section.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mean cross-sectional area $A$ of the wire in m².
Determine the Young modulus $E$ of the wire in GPa.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $E$.
Explain the purpose of the reference wire and why orthogonal micrometer readings are taken at three places.
parts.expectedAnswer: an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while orthogonal micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty
workingSteps: Identical reference wire cancels ceiling sag and thermal expansion equally on both scales.
Orthogonal readings at 3 positions check circularity and reduce random error in d².

items.stem: A marine thruster rotor of moment of inertia 3.60 kg m² reverses from $+20.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ to $-10.0\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ in 1.80 s under a uniform braking-and-reversing pulse. What is the magnitude of the mean external torque acting on the rotor?
items.workedSolution: $|\Delta L| = I|\omega_2 - \omega_1| = 3.60(30.0) = 108\text{ N m s}$. Mean torque $|T| = \frac{|\Delta L|}{\Delta t} = \frac{108}{1.80} = 60.0 N m$.

markScheme.criterion: Magnitude of mean torque equals 60.0 N m.

items.stem: Engineers evaluate a composite flywheel of moment of inertia 1.90 kg m² operating between 580 rad s⁻¹ and 240 rad s⁻¹ inside a municipal hybrid bus of total mass 1.15e+3 kg. On a test incline of road length 200 m rising 15.0 m vertically, the mean resistive drag force is 220 N. Take $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = 2.65 × 10⁵ J$. (b) $\Delta E_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.69 × 10⁵ J$. (c) Subtracting drag work 4.40 × 10⁴ J and dividing by $mg$ gives $h_{\max} = 19.6 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_{\max}^2 - \omega_{\min}^2)$.
Obtains 2.65 × 10⁵ J.
Uses $mgh$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Obtains 1.69 × 10⁵ J.
Computes drag work $F_{\mathrm{d}}s$ and subtracts from flywheel energy release.
Equates remaining energy to $mg h_{\max}$.
Obtains $h_{\max} = 19.6 m$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy released by the flywheel as it slows across its operating speed range.
Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy during the test incline.
workingSteps: Use $\Delta E_{\mathrm{p}} = m g \Delta h$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

parts.prompt: Assuming zero transmission losses and constant resistive work along the same road length, determine the maximum vertical height this flywheel energy release could lift the vehicle.
workingSteps: Work against drag $W_{\mathrm{d}} = F_{\mathrm{d}} s = 4.40 × 10⁴ J$.
Remaining energy for height gain $mgh_{\max} = \Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} - W_{\mathrm{d}}$.

items.stem: Of weight 1600 N, a railway sleeper pack slides down an embankment chute at a constant speed of 5 m s⁻¹. The ramp has length 30 m along the slope and a vertical drop of 7.5 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses F_f = W sin θ = W h / L at constant velocity.
Obtains 400 N.
Applies P = F_f v.
Obtains 2.00 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu².
Obtains 5.24 m s⁻¹.
Applies T = mg + mu²/L.
Obtains 20.6 N.
Conserves momentum v = mu/(m+M) then uses h = v²/(2g).
Obtains 0.137 m.

items.stem: Swinging down from rest with its 0.9 m string initially horizontal in a Charpy-style swing rig, a cast-iron hammer bob (mass 2.8 kg) embeds into stationary a deformable putty mass (mass 5.6 kg) at the bottom. Take the acceleration of free fall to be g = 9.81 m s⁻². How much mechanical energy is dissipated during the sticking collision?
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 4.20 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 1.40 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.100 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 16.5 J. Target = 16.5 J.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 16.5 J (B).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a submarine-simulator bulkhead inspection hatch of length L = 1.2 m and mass 18 kg is smoothly hinged at O to a vertical wall and held horizontally in static equilibrium. Because of an internal reinforcing frame, its centre of gravity G lies 0.46 m from hinge O. A single steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at an angle of 36° to the vertical (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 83.67 N ≈ 83.7 N. (b) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (c)(i) R_x = 49.18 N, R_y = 108.9 N, so R = 119.5 N ≈ 119 N. (c)(ii) α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 65.69° ≈ 65.7° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Στ = 0 about O using T cos(angle to vertical) × L = m g x_G.
Obtains T = 83.67 N (83.7 N) matching 84 N.
Identifies horizontal component of angled cable tension directed toward the wall.
States hinge must exert an equal opposite horizontal force away from the wall for ΣF_x = 0.
Computes R_x = 49.18 N and R_y = 108.9 N and applies Pythagoras.
Resultant hinge reaction magnitude R = 119 N.
Uses tan α = R_y / R_x with both hinge components.
Direction α = 65.7° above the horizontal.

items.stem: Released from rest at the anchor of a stretchable nylon hawser (natural length 4.6 m) in a dry-test tower, a marine mooring weight of mass 13 kg falls freely to point A where the cord becomes taut, then stretches the cord by 0.9 m over 0.24 s before reaching instantaneous rest at B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 9.50 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (13 × 9.50) / 0.24 = 515 N.
Obtains 642 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 1.56 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Writes T_max − mg = m v_max² / r at the lowest point.
Obtains 9.21 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The three-stage diagram shows a calibration steel ball of mass 10.5 kg dropped from rest at the support of a Hookean rubber cord (natural length 1.8 m), reaching A taut and extending a further 0.55 m over 0.38 s to rest at lowest point B. Assume gravitational field strength g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the spring constant of a Hookean rubber cord?
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 1.8 + 0.55 = 2.35 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 1.60 × 10³ N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 879 N. Target = 1.60 × 10³ N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (1.8 + 0.55) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 1.60 × 10³ N m⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a timber-mill log-handling tower crane has total length L = 24 m and mass 700 kg, supported on a vertical mast pivot P located 5.5 m from the rear end A. A concrete counterweight of mass 2600 kg sits 4.7 m to the left of P (0.8 m from A). The centre of gravity G of the boom itself lies 3.5 m to the right of P (9 m from A), and the hoist hook hangs 17.5 m to the right of P (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) M_cw = 1.199 × 10⁵ N m ≈ 1.20 × 10⁵ N m. (b) Equating clockwise and anticlockwise moments about P gives m_max = 558.3 kg ≈ 558 kg. (c) Vertical force balance yields R = 3.785 × 10⁴ N ≈ 3.78 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses M = m g d with counterweight mass and lever arm from P.
Counterweight moment = 1.20 × 10⁵ N m.
Subtracts boom self-weight moment from counterweight moment and divides by g × load lever arm.
Maximum safe load mass = 558 kg.
Applies vertical force balance summing counterweight, boom, and load weights.
Upward mast reaction R = 3.78 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: The diagram shows glider X of mass 1.6 kg moving right at 6 m s⁻¹ toward stationary glider Y of mass 0.8 kg on a horizontal frictionless air track; after collision, glider Y travels right at 5.06 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of glider X immediately after the collision?

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 3.47 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: In a rebound impact on a polished ice test channel, sled X (mass 2 kg, initial speed 15 m s⁻¹ right) hits stationary sled Y (mass 5.2 kg), which moves right at 6.67 m s⁻¹. What is the total kinetic energy of the two bodies immediately after impact?
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (2)(15) = (2)v_X + (5.2)(6.67) gives v_X = -2.34 m s⁻¹ (2.34 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(2)(2.34)² + ½(5.2)(6.67)² = 121 J. Energy lost = 225 J − K_f = 104 J. Target = 121 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 2.34 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 121 J (B).

items.stem: At the bottom of a vertical circle of radius 1.7 m in a vertical rotation stand, a telemetry capsule of mass 1.7 kg travels at 9.5 m s⁻¹ while attached to a high-tensile cord. Take the acceleration of free fall to be g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in a high-tensile cord.
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.7 × 9.5² / 1.7 = 90.2 N, so T = 90.2 + 1.7 × 9.8 = 107 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 107 N (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: Launched from a spring-loaded catapult across a level arena floor, a robotics arena sphere has an initial speed of 42 m s⁻¹ at 28° above the horizontal. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.
items.workedSolution: (a) v_apex = 42 × cos 28°. Answer: 37.1 m s⁻¹. (b) u_y = 42 × sin 28° = 19.7 m s⁻¹. h_max = u_y² / (2 × 9.8). Answer: 19.8 m. (c) T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 4.02 s. R = 37.1 × T. Answer: 149 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 37.1 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 19.8 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 149 m.

items.stem: In a workshop statics test, a solar-panel mounting rail AB of length L = 4.4 m and mass 16 kg has its centre of gravity G at 2.2 m from end A. items.workedSolution: (a) The moment of a force is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. (b) Moment balance about P gives d = 0.3307 m left of P, so distance from end B is 3.151 m ≈ 3.15 m.

Converts cleanly to distance from end B = 3.15 m.

items.stem: On a level low-friction dynamics rail, cart X of mass 3 kg moves to the right at 9 m s⁻¹ and collides head-on with cart Y of mass 1.2 kg moving to the left at 5.5 m s⁻¹ (arrow on Y not shown). Immediately after impact, cart Y moves to the right at 1.5 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) p_before = 3 × 9 + 1.2 × (−5.5) = 20.4 kg m s⁻¹. Answer: 20.4 kg m s⁻¹ to the right. (b) v_X = (20.4 − 1.2 × 1.5) / 3 = 6.20 m s⁻¹. Answer: 6.20 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_X u_X − m_Y |u_Y| with correct signs.
Obtains 20.4 kg m s⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a rooftop HVAC maintenance walkway beam of total length L = 4.8 m and mass 36 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is positioned 0.8 m from its left end, and support B is 2.2 m to the right of A, leaving an unsupported right-hand overhang of 1.8 m. A technician of mass 48 kg initially stands 2.5 m from the left end of the plank (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B give F₁ = 203.3 N ≈ 203 N. (b) Vertical equilibrium gives F₂ = 620.7 N ≈ 621 N. (c) the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases. (d) Setting F₁ = 0 about B yields d_tip = 0.4500 m ≈ 0.450 m.

markScheme.criterion: Takes moments about B summing plank and technician anticlockwise moments.
Support A reaction F₁ = 203 N.
Support B reaction F₂ = 621 N via vertical force balance.
States that the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
Sets F₁ = 0 and equates clockwise overhang moment to restoring plank moment about B.
Tipping distance past B = 0.450 m.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about support B, calculate the upward reaction force F₁ at support A while the technician is at the initial position.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment of F₁ about B = F₁ × 2.2.

parts.prompt: Deduce the upward reaction force F₂ at support B.
State qualitatively how the reaction forces at supports A and B change as the technician walks slowly toward the right-hand overhang.
parts.expectedAnswer: As the technician moves toward the overhang, the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
workingSteps: Explain that shifting weight toward support B reduces the anticlockwise moment about B so support A carries less load while support B carries more.

parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum distance past support B that the technician can walk onto the overhang before the plank begins to tip.
workingSteps: At the tipping limit, F₁ = 0; take moments about B: 48 g d_tip = 36 g (0.6000).

items.stem: During a range trial on a level demonstration track, a lecture-hall steel ball leaves a floor-mounted spring cannon at 32 m s⁻¹ and 60° above the horizontal. Take the acceleration of free fall to be g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the total time of flight before returning to a level demonstration track?
items.workedSolution: u_y = 32 sin 60° = 27.7 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 32 cos 60° = 16.0 m s⁻¹. Flight time T = 2u_y / 9.81 = 5.65 s; horizontal range R = u_x T = 90.4 m. Target = 5.65 s.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves orthogonal components accurately to obtain 5.65 s (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes time to reach the apex u sin θ / g rather than full time of flight.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Swaps sin θ and cos θ when resolving vertical launch speed.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses total speed u instead of vertical component u sin θ.

items.stem: During proving-ground tests, an airport baggage tractor of mass 1400 kg accelerates along a level straight so a cab-mounted pendulum bob deflects by 34° from the vertical, climbs a straight 14° incline at constant speed, negotiates a flat semicircular curve of radius 75 m (coefficient of static friction 0.5), and finally coasts along the semicircle from 18 m s⁻¹ against a constant 470 N resistance toward the concourse stop. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses T sin θ = ma and T cos θ = mg => a = g tan θ.
Obtains 6.61 m s⁻².
Applies μ_s mg = m v_max² / R.
Obtains 19.2 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts resistive work F_res(πR) from initial kinetic energy ½mu².
Obtains 12.9 m s⁻¹.

Calculate the maximum speed on the flat semicircular road without sliding.
Calculate the speed with which an airport baggage tractor reaches the concourse stop at the end of the semicircular coast.

items.stem: A $1400\text{ kg}$ car travelling at $12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ crashes into a barrier and comes to rest in $0.300\text{ s}$ with its crumple zone deforming.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta p = 1.68 \times 10^4\text{ N s}$; $F = 5.60 \times 10^4\text{ N}$. (b) same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants.

markScheme.criterion: Impulse $= 1.68 × 10⁴ N s$.
Apply $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Average force $= 5.60 × 10⁴ N$.
Same change in momentum (equal area under F–t graph).
Longer impact time reduces average force F = Δp/Δt on occupants.

parts.expectedAnswer: Impulse $= 1.68 × 10⁴ N s$; average force $= 5.60 × 10⁴ N$

parts.prompt: Explain with reference to the force–time graph why extending collision time protects passengers.
parts.expectedAnswer: The area under the $F\text{–}t$ graph equals impulse $\Delta p$, so same change in momentum over a longer impact time reduces average force on occupants.
workingSteps: Area under F-t is fixed Δp; longer Δt gives smaller average/peak force F = Δp/Δt.

items.stem: A reinforced mortar rainwater gutter of length L = 3.10 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 18.0 cm and inner diameter d = 10.0 cm and average density ρ = 2250 kg m⁻³. The component is uniform along its length so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. A workshop lifting winch rated at electrical input power 360 W and efficiency 72% is later attached to end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 8.796 × 10⁻³ m², V = A L = 0.02727 m³, m = ρ V = 61.36 kg ≈ 61.4 kg. (b) W = 601.9 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 300.9 N ≈ 301 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.550 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 932.9 J ≈ 933 J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.72 × 360 = 259.2 W, so t = 932.9 / 259.2 = 3.599 s ≈ 3.60 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes semi-annular cross-section A = (π/8)(D² − d²) = 8.796 × 10⁻³ m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.02727 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 61.36 kg rounding clearly to 61.4 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.10 = m g × 1.550.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 301 N (4 s.f. 300.9 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.550 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 933 J (4 s.f. 932.9 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 259.2 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 3.60 s (4 s.f. 3.599 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A carved granite drainage trough of length L = 2.40 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 24.0 cm and inner diameter d = 14.0 cm and average density ρ = 2650 kg m⁻³. The component is uniform along its length so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. A electric gantry hoist rated at electrical input power 540 W and efficiency 78% is later attached to end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01492 m², V = A L = 0.03581 m³, m = ρ V = 94.91 kg ≈ 94.9 kg. (b) W = 931.0 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 465.5 N ≈ 466 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.200 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1117 J ≈ 1.12e+3 J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.78 × 540 = 421.2 W, so t = 1117 / 421.2 = 2.653 s ≈ 2.65 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 0.01492 m², volume V = 0.03581 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 94.91 kg confirming 94.9 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.40 = m g × 1.200.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 466 N (4 s.f. 465.5 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.200 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.12e+3 J (4 s.f. 1117 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 421.2 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 2.65 s (4 s.f. 2.653 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

items.stem: During Required Practical 3, a steel sphere drops through two light gates separated by height $h$. Plotting $2h/t$ against $t$ yields a straight line of gradient 9.74 m s⁻² and vertical intercept 2.28 m s⁻¹. What was the speed $u$ of the sphere as it passed the upper light gate?
items.workedSolution: From $h = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, rearranging gives $2h/t = gt + 2u$. Thus $g = 9.74$ m s⁻², $u = 2.28 / 2 = 1.14 m s⁻¹$, and percentage difference $= |9.74 - 9.81|/9.81 \times 100\% = 0.714%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates initialSpeedU $= 1.14 m s⁻¹$.

items.stem: A student using an electromagnet and trapdoor consistently obtains $g = 9.42$ m s⁻² across repeated trials with a dense steel sphere. Which systematic error best explains this result?
items.workedSolution: RP3 evaluation: Residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

markScheme.criterion: Residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

items.stem: A student is tasked with measuring the Young modulus of a long steel wire using Searle's dual-wire apparatus suspended from a rigid ceiling beam.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Wear safety goggles in case the taut wire snaps and place a sand tray or cushioned pad directly beneath the hanging slotted masses, keeping feet clear. Hang a long thin test wire alongside an identical reference wire carrying a small constant mass from the same rigid beam so ceiling sag and thermal expansion cancel equally. Check micrometer zero error, then use the ratchet to measure wire diameter in perpendicular directions at least three positions along the wire; average d and compute A = πd²/4. Measure original length L from clamp to Vernier marker with a metre ruler after applying a small initial load to remove kinks. Add known masses incrementally (F = mg, g = 9.81 m s⁻²), recording Vernier extension e at eye level, then record extensions while unloading to verify the elastic limit was not exceeded. Plot F against e, draw a best-fit line through the linear elastic region, determine gradient from > 50% span, and evaluate E = (L / A) × gradient.

markScheme.criterion: States safety precautions: wear safety goggles for snapping wire and place a sand tray/cushion under slotted masses.
Explains that the identical reference wire compensates both ceiling-beam sag and thermal expansion.
Measures diameter using a zero-checked micrometer with ratchet at >= 3 places in orthogonal directions to find A = πd²/4.
Applies a small initial straightening load, measures original length L with a metre ruler, and records incremental Vernier extensions e for loads F = mg.
Takes unloading readings to confirm the wire returns to original readings (elastic limit not exceeded).
Plots F against e (or stress against strain) and extracts E = (L / A) × gradient from a best-fit straight line.

parts.prompt: Describe a detailed, safe experimental method to obtain an accurate value for the Young modulus, explaining all measurements, instrument techniques, error controls, and graphical analysis. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Wear safety goggles and place a sand tray beneath the slotted masses; an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while orthogonal micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty; measure unstretched length L with a metre ruler, apply incremental loads F = mg while reading Vernier extensions during both loading and unloading, plot F against e, and obtain E = (L/A) × gradient.
workingSteps: Level 1: Safety goggles + sand tray beneath slotted masses; long thin test wire and identical reference wire.
Level 2: Micrometer with ratchet (zero-error checked) at >= 3 orthogonal pairs for d -> A = πd²/4; ruler for L; initial straightening load + Vernier extension readings.
Level 3: Repeat readings during unloading to confirm elastic limit, plot F vs e (straight line through origin), compute E = L × gradient / A.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a workshop overhead lighting conduit bar of total length L = 2.8 m and mass 8 kg hangs horizontally in equilibrium from two light vertical ceiling wires attached at A and B, separated by 2.1 m. Its centre of gravity G lies 0.76 m to the right of attachment A and 1.34 m to the left of attachment B (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the tension in wire A (T₁)?
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: T₁_y × 2.1 = 8 × 9.81 × 1.34 ⇒ T₁_y = 50.08 N, T₂_y = 28.40 N. For vertical wires, T₁ = 50.08 N ≈ 50.1 N and T₂ = 28.40 N ≈ 28.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct wire tension = 50.1 N.

items.stem: Two equal and opposite parallel forces, each of magnitude F = 74 N, are applied to the ends of a laboratory torsion-head brass lever of length d = 0.36 m, each inclined at 55° to the bar, as illustrated in the diagram. What is the magnitude of the torque of this couple?
items.workedSolution: Perpendicular separation between the parallel lines of action is d_perp = d sin 55° = 0.2949 m. Torque of the couple: T = F d_perp = 74 × 0.2949 = 21.82 N m ≈ 21.8 N m.

markScheme.criterion: Correct couple torque = 21.8 N m.

items.stem: The diagram depicts a transformer housing weighing 280 N moving at constant speed down a substation access slope of length 33 m and vertical height 10.6 m. What is the magnitude of the resistive force opposing motion along the slope?
items.workedSolution: At constant speed ΔE_k = 0. Potential energy lost = W h = 280 × 10.6 = 2.97 × 10³ J. Parallel equilibrium gives F_res = W sin θ = W h / L = 89.9 N. Target = 89.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ = 10.6/33 and zero net force to obtain 89.9 N (A).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a studio spotlight cantilevered wall boom is a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 2 m and mass 10 kg smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 6.5 kg hangs so that its centre of gravity acts 1.5 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at an angle of 32° above the horizontal rod (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about O give T = 182.8 N ≈ 183 N. (b) Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos θ = 155.0 N ≈ 155 N. (c) Vertical balance: R_y = W_total − T sin θ = 64.99 N ≈ 65.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Writes full moment balance about hinge O including both rod and sign moments with T sin θ.
Evaluates T = 182.8 N (183 N) showing agreement with 1.8e+2 N.
Applies horizontal equilibrium R_x = T cos θ.
R_x = 155 N away from the wall.
Applies vertical equilibrium R_y = W_total − T sin θ.
R_y = 65.0 N upwards.

parts.prompt: By taking moments about hinge O, show clearly that the tension T in the angled wire is approximately 1.8e+2 N.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment about O = (10 × 1 + 6.5 × 1.5) × 9.81 = 193.7 N m.
T = 182.8 N ≈ 183 N, which rounds to 1.8e+2 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the horizontal component of the force exerted by hinge O on the rod.
workingSteps: Horizontal equilibrium: R_x = T cos 32° = 182.8 × cos 32° = 155.0 N ≈ 155 N away from the wall.

parts.prompt: Calculate the vertical component of the force exerted by hinge O on the rod.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium: R_y = W − T sin 32° = 64.99 N ≈ 65.0 N upwards.

items.stem: In Required Practical 4 on a annealed copper wire of length $(2.10 \pm 0.002)$ m, orthogonal micrometer readings give mean diameters 0.48 mm, 0.46 mm, and 0.47 mm (uncertainty $\pm 0.01$ mm). The gradient of the $F$ against $e$ graph has percentage uncertainty 1.8%. Calculate the total percentage uncertainty in the Young modulus $E$.
items.workedSolution: Mean diameter $d = 0.47$ mm gives $A = \pi d^2/4 = 1.73 × 10⁻⁷ m²$. $E = L \times \mathrm{grad} / A = 119 GPa$. Percentage uncertainty $\%\Delta E = \%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad} = 0.0952 + 2(2.13) + 1.8 = 6.15%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates pctUncE $= 6.15%$.

items.stem: A spinning orbital probe with extended telemetry booms has moment of inertia 16.0 kg m² and spins at 3.00 rad s⁻¹ with zero external torque. Internal actuators draw the booms inward, reducing the moment of inertia to 6.40 kg m².
items.workedSolution: (a) $\omega_2 = 7.50 rad s⁻¹$. (b) Work done $= \frac{1}{2}I_2\omega_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2 = 108 J$. (c) Internal radial forces do positive work pulling masses inward so rotational kinetic energy increases.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$.
Obtains $\omega_2 = 7.50 rad s⁻¹$.
Calculates initial rotational KE $\frac{1}{2}I_1\omega_1^2$.
Calculates final rotational KE $\frac{1}{2}I_2\omega_2^2$ and finds difference.
Obtains internal work $= 108 J$.
Explains that radial actuator forces produce zero torque about the spin axis.
States that internal radial forces do positive work pulling the pods inward.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final angular velocity of the probe.
Calculate the work done by the internal winches in retracting the booms.
Explain why rotational kinetic energy increases even though no external torque acts on the probe.
parts.expectedAnswer: Internal radial forces do positive work pulling masses inward so rotational kinetic energy increases.
workingSteps: Internal radial forces pass through the axis and create zero external torque, leaving angular momentum unchanged.
Because the winches pull the pods inward against their outward tendency, internal radial forces do positive work increasing kinetic energy.

items.stem: A 1350 kg delivery van uses a KERS flywheel to climb a ramp rising 16.0 m vertically over a road length of 250 m against a mean resistive force of 280 N. Take $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$. If the flywheel slows from 620 rad s⁻¹ to 260 rad s⁻¹ with zero transmission loss, calculate the minimum moment of inertia required.
items.workedSolution: Required energy $E = mgh + F_{\mathrm{d}}s = 1350(9.81)(16.0) + 280(250) = 2.82 × 10⁵ J$. Setting $\frac{1}{2}I(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2) = E$ gives $I = \frac{2E}{620^2 - 260^2} = 1.78 kg m²$.

markScheme.criterion: Minimum flywheel moment of inertia equals 1.78 kg m².

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes gravitational potential gain $mgh$ but ignores work done against drag $F_{\mathrm{d}}s$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses $(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$ instead of $(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2)$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of $2$ when rearranging $\Delta E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2)$.

items.stem: Descending a greased timber way of length 22 m and vertical drop 8.8 m at a steady speed of 6.5 m s⁻¹, a shipyard launch block has weight 900 N. At what rate is mechanical energy converted into thermal energy?
items.workedSolution: At constant speed, friction balances downslope weight: F_f = W(h/L) = 900 × (8.8/22) = 360 N. Rate of thermal energy generation P = F_f v = 2.34 × 10³ W. Target = 2.34 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_f = Wh/L and P = F_f v to obtain 2.34 × 10³ W (B).

items.stem: The diagram shows a brass impact sphere of mass 0.3 kg released from a horizontal 1.4 m string in a laboratory swing frame toward stationary a wax capture block of mass 0.3 kg at the bottom. Assume gravitational field strength g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the tension in the string immediately before a brass impact sphere strikes a wax capture block?
items.workedSolution: Just before collision u² = 2gL => u = 5.24 m s⁻¹. Radial Newton second law T − mg = mu²/L = 2mg gives T = 3mg = 8.83 N. Momentum conservation gives v = mu/(m+M) = 2.62 m s⁻¹. Target = 8.83 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates quarter-swing dynamics and radial/tangential laws to obtain 8.83 N (C).

items.stem: In a momentum demonstration stand, a lead-filled test bob of mass 2 kg attached to a light inextensible string of length 2.1 m is released from rest with the string horizontal. At the lowest point of its swing it collides with and sticks to stationary a Velcro-lined receiver of mass 2.4 kg. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mgL = ½mu² => u = √(2gL).
Obtains 6.42 m s⁻¹.
Finds v = mu/(m+M) from momentum conservation and evaluates ½mu² − ½(m+M)v².
Obtains 22.5 J.
Applies h = v² / (2g).
Obtains 0.434 m.

items.stem: The diagram shows the rotor of a high-speed textile winding drum. Its central hub has moment of inertia 1.60 kg m² and carries 6 rim masses of 1.40 kg each at radius 0.350 m. During a test run lasting 10.0 s, the rotational speed changes uniformly from 14.0 rev s⁻¹ to 2.00 rev s⁻¹ while a constant bearing friction torque of 2.00 N m opposes rotation.
items.workedSolution: (a) $I = 2.63 kg m²$. (b) $|\alpha| = \frac{2\pi|f_2 - f_1|}{t} = 7.54 rad s⁻²$. (c) Applied torque $T_{\mathrm{app}} = 17.8 N m$. (d) Peak power $P_{\max} = T_{\mathrm{app}}\omega_{\max} = 1.57e+3 W$.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $I = I_{\mathrm{hub}} + \sum m r^2$ with squared radius.
Obtains $I = 2.63 kg m²$.
Converts $\text{rev s}^{-1}$ to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ via $2\pi$ and divides change by $t$.
Obtains $|\alpha| = 7.54 rad s⁻²$.
Combines $I|\alpha|$ with bearing friction torque in the correct sense.
Obtains applied torque $= 17.8 N m$.
Applies $P = T\omega$ at the highest angular speed.
Obtains maximum power $= 1.57e+3 W$.

items.stem: The diagram shows an instrumented cargo crate of mass 4.5 kg starting from rest and descending 5 m down a straight steel loading chute angled at 28°, attaining 4.54 m s⁻¹ at the bottom. Assume gravitational field strength g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the coefficient of dynamic friction μ_d between an instrumented cargo crate and a straight steel loading chute?
items.workedSolution: Gravitational potential energy lost ΔE_p = mgL sin 28° = 104 J. Final kinetic energy E_k = ½(4.5)(4.54)² = 46.4 J. Frictional energy loss W_f = ΔE_p − E_k = 57.1 J. Since W_f = μ(mg cos 28°)L, μ = 0.294. Target = 0.294.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔE_p − E_k and normal reaction mg cos 28° accurately to obtain 0.294 (B).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a warehouse loading-chute steel baffle plate of length L = 2.2 m and mass 32 kg is smoothly hinged at O to a vertical wall and held horizontally in static equilibrium. Because of an internal reinforcing frame, its centre of gravity G lies 0.88 m from hinge O. A single steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at an angle of 28° to the vertical (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). At what angle above the horizontal does the resultant reaction force R from hinge O act on the door?
items.workedSolution: Moments about O: T cos 28° × 2.2 = 32 × 9.81 × 0.88 ⇒ T = 142.2 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T sin 28° = 66.77 N. Vertical balance: R_y = 32 × 9.81 − T cos 28° = 188.4 N. Resultant R = √(R_x² + R_y²) = 199.8 N ≈ 200 N, at angle α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 70.48° ≈ 70.5° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 70.5°.

items.stem: The diagram illustrates a mountaineering test mass of mass 2 kg released at the support of a dynamic climbing rope (natural length 2.6 m), becoming taut at A and decelerating to rest at B (extension 1.2 m) over 0.33 s. Assume gravitational field strength g = 9.81 m s⁻². What mean force does a dynamic climbing rope exert between A and B?
items.workedSolution: Speed when taut at A: v_A = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.6) = 7.14 m s⁻¹ downward. Taking upward positive, (F_mean − mg)Δt = 0 − (−mv_A), so F_mean = mv_A / 0.33 + 2(9.81) = 62.9 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = mv_A with v_A = √(2gL) to obtain 62.9 N (D).

items.stem: During a tensile limit test in a vertical circular test rig, a steel sensor sphere of mass 1.2 kg swings on a light inextensible wire of length 1.2 m rated to 29 N maximum tension. Take the acceleration of free fall to be g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum speed at the bottom of the path.
items.workedSolution: Tension is greatest at the bottom where T_max − mg = m v_max² / r. Thus v_max = √[((29/1.2) − 9.81) × 1.2] = 4.15 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Solves T_max − mg = mv²/r to obtain 4.15 m s⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds g instead of subtracting g when rearranging T_max − mg = mv²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats vertical circular motion as horizontal, omitting weight mg at the lowest point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes minimum top-of-loop critical speed √(gr) instead of maximum safe bottom speed.

items.stem: In an overhead hoist beam, a crane overload test block of mass 5 kg is released from rest at the upper support of an elastic snubber line, which has natural unstretched length 3.2 m and obeys Hooke's law when taut. The cord first becomes taut at A and reaches maximum extension 0.45 m at lowest point B after an arrest interval of 0.28 s. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Uses free-fall relation v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 7.92 m s⁻¹.
Equates mg(L + x) = ½kx² over the complete vertical drop.
Obtains 1.77 × 10³ N m⁻¹.
Evaluates a_B = (kx − mg) / m.
Obtains 149 m s⁻².

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a high-rise tower construction crane has total length L = 16 m and mass 800 kg, supported on a vertical mast pivot P located 5.5 m from the rear end A. A concrete counterweight of mass 3800 kg sits 4.1 m to the left of P (1.4 m from A). The centre of gravity G of the boom itself lies 4 m to the right of P (9.5 m from A), and the hoist hook hangs 10 m to the right of P (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the maximum safe load weight that can be suspended from the hook without producing a net clockwise tipping moment about P?
items.workedSolution: Anticlockwise counterweight moment about P: M_cw = 3800 × 9.81 × 4.1 = 1.528 × 10⁵ N m. Clockwise boom moment: M_boom = 800 × 9.81 × 4 = 3.139 × 10⁴ N m. Remaining clockwise moment available for load: W_max × 10 = 1.214 × 10⁵ N m ⇒ W_max = 1.214 × 10⁴ N ≈ 1.21 × 10⁴ N, m_max = W_max / 9.81 = 1238 kg ≈ 1.24e+3 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct maximum safe load weight = 1.21 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: Along a smooth glass collision groove, trolley X of mass 2.8 kg travels to the right at 9 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary trolley Y of mass 1.6 kg. Immediately after impact, trolley Y moves to the right at 8.12 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies m_X u_X = m_X v_X + m_Y v_Y.
Obtains 4.36 m s⁻¹.
Sums ½m_X v_X² + ½m_Y v_Y².
Obtains 79.4 J.
Subtracts K_f from K_i = ½m_X u_X².
Obtains 34.0 J.

items.stem: In a chute calibration, a stage ballast crate of mass 3.5 kg descends 10 m from rest down an angled loading board inclined at 30° and exits the base at 5.45 m s⁻¹ under constant friction. Take the acceleration of free fall to be g = 9.81 m s⁻². If the same object is instead released from rest halfway down an angled loading board, what speed does it reach at the bottom?
items.workedSolution: Energy dissipated W_f = mgL sin 30° − ½mv² = 120 J. Constant friction force F_f = W_f / 10 = 12.0 N. Released halfway down at unchanged acceleration a, v_half = v / √2 = 3.85 m s⁻¹. Target = 3.85 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies work-energy / constant-acceleration scaling on the incline to obtain 3.85 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: In a vertical loop frame, a compact lead bob of mass 1.1 kg is attached to a light steel cable of length 2 m and moves in a vertical circle, passing through the lowest point with speed 7.5 m s⁻¹. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F_c = mv² / r.
Obtains 30.9 N.
Applies T − mg = F_c => T = F_c + mg.
Obtains 41.7 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant centripetal force on a compact lead bob at the lowest point.
Hence calculate the tension in a light steel cable at the lowest point.

items.stem: Referring to the launch of a tracer polymer pellet from a ground discharge tube at 30 m s⁻¹ and 24° above a horizontal test paddock: Take the acceleration of free fall to be g = 9.8 m s⁻². What maximum vertical height above a horizontal test paddock does it reach?
items.workedSolution: At the apex v_y = 0 while horizontal velocity remains constant at v_apex = u cos 24° = 27.4 m s⁻¹. Maximum height h_max = (u sin 24°)² / (2g) = 7.60 m. Target = 7.60 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_y = 0 and constant v_x = u cos 24° at apex to obtain 7.60 m (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts all initial kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy, forgetting non-zero horizontal speed u cos θ at the apex.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses horizontal component u cos θ instead of vertical component u sin θ in h = u_y² / (2g).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of two in the denominator of h_max = u_y² / (2g).

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a museum exhibition display beam AB of total length L = 4.4 m and mass 16 kg is uniform, with its centre of gravity G at its midpoint (2.2 m from end A). The beam rests horizontally in equilibrium on a sharp pivot P positioned 1.67 m from end A when a counterbalance block of unknown mass is placed 0.33 m from end A (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What mass of counterbalance block is required to hold the beam horizontally in equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: Take moments about pivot P. Lever arm of beam CG is d_G = 2.2 − 1.67 = 0.5300 m. Lever arm of counterbalance is d_load = 1.67 − 0.33 = 1.340 m. Balancing moments: m_load g d_load = m_beam g d_G ⇒ m_load = (16 × 0.5300) / 1.340 = 6.328 kg ≈ 6.33 kg. Vertical equilibrium gives R = (m_beam + m_load)g = (16 + 6.328) × 9.81 = 219.0 N ≈ 219 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct balancing mass m_load = 6.33 kg.

items.stem: Along a smooth marshalling test track, wagon X of mass 2 kg travelling right at 13 m s⁻¹ meets wagon Y of mass 3.6 kg travelling left at 6 m s⁻¹ (not drawn). After impact wagon Y rebounds right at 4 m s⁻¹. What is the post-collision velocity of wagon X?
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward as positive: p_before = (2)(13) + (3.6)(−6) = 4.40 kg m s⁻¹. From p_before = (2)v_X + (3.6)(4), v_X = -5.00 m s⁻¹, which is 5.00 m s⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Uses signed head-on momentum p_before = 4.40 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 5.00 m s⁻¹ to the left (C).

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a warehouse cantilevered staging board of total length L = 5.4 m and mass 48 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is positioned 0.6 m from its left end, and support B is 3.2 m to the right of A, leaving an unsupported right-hand overhang of 1.6 m. A technician of mass 66 kg initially stands 2.1 m from the left end of the plank (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). How far past support B onto the overhang can the technician walk before the plank begins to tip?
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about B: F₁ × 3.2 = (48 × 1.100 + 66 × 1.700) × 9.81 ⇒ F₁ = 505.8 N ≈ 506 N. At tipping (F₁ = 0): m_load × d_tip = m_beam × (x_B − x_G) ⇒ d_tip = (48 × 1.100) / 66 = 0.8000 m ≈ 0.800 m. At the very tip (overhang 1.6 m): m_end = (48 × 1.100) / 1.6 = 33.00 kg ≈ 33.0 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solver-verified answer = 0.800 m.

items.stem: On horizontal farmland, a ground-level nozzle launches an irrigation water packet from ground level at speed 20 m s⁻¹ and angle 38° above the horizontal. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates u_y = u sin θ.
Obtains 12.3 m s⁻¹.
Applies T = 2u_y / g.
Obtains 2.51 s.
Multiplies u cos θ by flight time T.
Obtains 39.6 m.

items.stem: During multi-stage proving trials, an instrumented test truck of mass 1700 kg accelerates horizontally so a ceiling-suspended plumb bob hangs at 38° to the vertical, later climbs a 8° grade at steady speed, traverses a flat semicircular bend of radius 70 m (static friction coefficient 0.8), and coasts from 22 m s⁻¹ against a 620 N resistive force toward the terminal bay. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the maximum speed on the flat semicircular curve of radius 70 m without skidding?
items.workedSolution: Plumb-bob equilibrium: T sin 38° = ma and T cos 38° = mg => a = g tan 38° = 7.66 m s⁻². Flat curve limit: v_max = √(0.8 × 9.8 × 70) = 23.4 m s⁻¹. Coasting stop distance: s = ½(1700)(22)² / 620 = 664 m. Target = 23.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates target vehicle mechanics relation cleanly to obtain 23.4 m s⁻¹ (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the static friction coefficient μ_s in μ_s mg = mv²/R.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by μ_s instead of multiplying by μ_s.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes v² = μ_s g R without taking the square root.

items.stem: A student wishes to calculate the acceleration at point P and total distance fallen between release and point Q on the curved skydiver velocity–time graph. Which method is physically valid?
items.workedSolution: Because acceleration decreases continuously as drag grows, constant acceleration equations are invalid; use tangent gradient for acceleration and area under the $v\text{–}t$ graph for distance. Therefore option A is correct: constant acceleration equations are invalid so use tangent gradient and area under velocity time graph.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: constant acceleration equations are invalid so use tangent gradient and area under velocity time graph.

options.label: A
options.text: Because air resistance varies with speed, constant acceleration equations are invalid so use tangent gradient and area under velocity time graph

options.label: B
options.text: Because air resistance varies with speed, substitute g into s = ut + half a t squared across the whole curve
options.distractorRationale: Explicit AQA reject rule: SUVAT equations are valid ONLY for constant (uniform) acceleration.

options.label: C
options.text: Because air resistance varies with speed, divide final terminal velocity by total time to get instantaneous acceleration at P
options.distractorRationale: v/t gives average acceleration over the whole interval, not instantaneous acceleration at P.

options.label: D
options.text: Because air resistance varies with speed, multiply the tangent gradient at P by total time to obtain distance fallen
options.distractorRationale: Distance fallen is the area under the v–t curve, not gradient × time.

items.stem: A non-uniform cast-iron ballast bar of length L = 2.20 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a rectangular cross-section of width w = 16.0 cm and thickness h = 8.0 cm and average density ρ = 7200 kg m⁻³. Internal reinforcement makes the component non-uniform so its centre of gravity G lies at distance x = 0.99 m from end A (as shown). A heavy foundry chain hoist rated at electrical input power 850 W and efficiency 84% is later attached to end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 0.01280 m², V = A L = 0.02816 m³, m = ρ V = 202.8 kg ≈ 203 kg. (b) W = 1989 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 895.0 N ≈ 895 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 0.9900 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1969 J ≈ 1.97e+3 J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.84 × 850 = 714.0 W, so t = 1969 / 714.0 = 2.758 s ≈ 2.76 s. (e) density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

markScheme.criterion: Computes cross-section A = w h = 0.01280 m² with cm → m conversion.
Calculates V = A L = 0.02816 m³ and substitutes m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 202.8 kg rounding clearly to 203 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 2.20 = m g × 0.9900.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 895 N (4 s.f. 895.0 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 0.9900 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.97e+3 J (4 s.f. 1969 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 714.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 2.76 s (4 s.f. 2.758 s).
States valid physical assumption: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

parts.prompt: Calculate the cross-sectional area and volume of the non-uniform cast-iron ballast bar, and show clearly that its mass is approximately 203 kg. [3]
By taking moments about end A, calculate the minimum vertical upward force F applied at end B required to just lift end B off the ground. [2]

Neglecting the initial height of the centre of gravity above the ground, calculate the minimum work done (gain in gravitational potential energy) to rotate the component until it stands vertically upright on end A. [2]
workingSteps: Vertical rise of centre of gravity G is Δh = x = 0.9900 m

parts.prompt: Calculate the minimum time taken for the 850 W hoist motor operating at 84% efficiency to stand the component upright. [2]
workingSteps: Useful output power P_out = η P_in = 0.84 × 850 = 714.0 W

parts.prompt: State one physical assumption made when using the gravitational potential energy change to calculate the minimum hoist time. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK synoptic evaluation rubric: density is uniform and negligible work is done against friction or giving kinetic energy to the beam.

items.stem: A glazed stoneware spillway channel of length L = 3.40 m rests horizontally on level ground (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). As shown in the figure, it has a semi-annular cross-section of outer diameter D = 19.0 cm and inner diameter d = 11.0 cm and average density ρ = 2320 kg m⁻³. The component is uniform along its length so its centre of gravity G lies at its midpoint. A hydraulic-electric yard winch rated at electrical input power 450 W and efficiency 74% is later attached to end B to stand the component vertically upright on end A.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 9.425 × 10⁻³ m², V = A L = 0.03204 m³, m = ρ V = 74.34 kg ≈ 74.3 kg. (b) W = 729.3 N; taking moments about A gives F = W × (x_G / L) = 364.7 N ≈ 365 N. (c) Centre of gravity rises by Δh = 1.700 m, so ΔE_p = m g Δh = 1240 J ≈ 1.24e+3 J. (d) Useful power P_out = 0.74 × 450 = 333.0 W, so t = 1240 / 333.0 = 3.723 s ≈ 3.72 s. (e) electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates cross-section A = 9.425 × 10⁻³ m², volume V = 0.03204 m³, and applies m = ρ V.
Shows 4 s.f. mass 74.34 kg confirming 74.3 kg.
Applies principle of moments about A: F × 3.40 = m g × 1.700.
Evaluates minimum lift force F = 365 N (4 s.f. 364.7 N).
Uses centre-of-gravity rise Δh = 1.700 m (not full length L) in ΔE_p = m g Δh.
Obtains work done = 1.24e+3 J (4 s.f. 1240 J).
Applies useful power P_out = η P_in = 333.0 W and t = ΔE_p / P_out.
Evaluates minimum hoist time = 3.72 s (4 s.f. 3.723 s).
Identifies electrical heating in motor windings and mechanical friction in hoist gears.
Links losses to thermal energy dissipated to the surroundings (electrical heating in the motor windings and friction in the hoist gears dissipate thermal energy to the surroundings).

items.stem: In Required Practical 3, a student drops a dense steel sphere through two light gates and plots $2h/t$ against $t$. The best-fit straight line has gradient 9.92 m s⁻² (with percentage uncertainty 1.8%) and vertical intercept 3.16 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $u = 3.16/2 = 1.58 m s⁻¹$. (b) $\Delta g = 0.179 m s⁻²$. (c) Percentage difference $= 1.12%$ (smaller than the 1.8% experimental uncertainty, so result is consistent with 9.81 m s⁻²). (d) use a plumb line to align the metre ruler vertically and plot two h over t against t so the gradient equals gravitational field strength independently of initial speed.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies vertical intercept equals $2u$.
Initial speed $u = 1.58 m s⁻¹$.
Multiplies measured $g$ by fractional uncertainty.
Absolute uncertainty $\Delta g = 0.179 m s⁻²$.
Computes $|g_{\mathrm{meas}} - 9.81|/9.81 \times 100\%$.
Percentage difference $= 1.12%$.
Uses a plumb line / set square against bench to ensure ruler is strictly vertical.
Shows $2h/t = gt + 2u$ keeps gradient equal to $g$ regardless of initial speed $u$.

items.stem: In the electromagnet-and-trapdoor arrangement of Required Practical 3, plotting drop height $h$ against $t^2$ produces a straight line of gradient 4.76 m s⁻². In an individual drop from $h = 1.15$ m, the digital timer records 0.4982 s because residual magnetism delays release by 14 ms.
items.workedSolution: (a) $g = 2 \times 4.76 = 9.52 m s⁻²$. (b) Percentage difference $= 2.96%$. (c) Single drop gives $g = 9.27 m s⁻²$. (d) residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $g = 2 \times \mathrm{gradient}$.
Measured $g = 9.52 m s⁻²$.
Divides absolute discrepancy by accepted $9.81$ m s⁻².
Percentage difference $= 2.96%$.
Substitutes into $g = 2h/t^2$.
Apparent $g = 9.27 m s⁻²$.
Residual magnetism delays release so recorded $t$ is systematically too large.
Suggests reducing electromagnet current / inserting paper spacer / using two light gates.

parts.expectedAnswer: residual magnetism in the electromagnet delays sphere release making the recorded fall time too large and producing a systematic underestimate of g; minimise by reducing electromagnet current to the minimum needed to hold the sphere or inserting a thin sheet of paper.

items.stem: A laboratory group uses a comparison-wire Vernier arrangement to investigate the elastic stiffness and Young modulus of an annealed copper wire.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Wear safety goggles in case the taut wire snaps and place a sand tray or cushioned pad directly beneath the hanging slotted masses, keeping feet clear. Hang a long thin test wire alongside an identical reference wire carrying a small constant mass from the same rigid beam so ceiling sag and thermal expansion cancel equally. Check micrometer zero error, then use the ratchet to measure wire diameter in perpendicular directions at least three positions along the wire; average d and compute A = πd²/4. Measure original length L from clamp to Vernier marker with a metre ruler after applying a small initial load to remove kinks. Add known masses incrementally (F = mg, g = 9.81 m s⁻²), recording Vernier extension e at eye level, then record extensions while unloading to verify the elastic limit was not exceeded. Plot F against e, draw a best-fit line through the linear elastic region, determine gradient from > 50% span, and evaluate E = (L / A) × gradient.

markScheme.criterion: States safety precautions: wear safety goggles for snapping wire and place a sand tray/cushion under slotted masses.
Explains that the identical reference wire compensates both ceiling-beam sag and thermal expansion.
Measures diameter using a zero-checked micrometer with ratchet at >= 3 places in orthogonal directions to find A = πd²/4.
Applies a small initial straightening load, measures original length L with a metre ruler, and records incremental Vernier extensions e for loads F = mg.
Takes unloading readings to confirm the wire returns to original readings (elastic limit not exceeded).
Plots F against e (or stress against strain) and extracts E = (L / A) × gradient from a best-fit straight line.

parts.prompt: Explain how the students should set up the apparatus safely, measure wire dimensions and extensions accurately, check elastic behaviour, and determine the Young modulus graphically. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Wear safety goggles and place a sand tray beneath the slotted masses; an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while orthogonal micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty; measure unstretched length L with a metre ruler, apply incremental loads F = mg while reading Vernier extensions during both loading and unloading, plot F against e, and obtain E = (L/A) × gradient.
workingSteps: Level 1: Safety goggles + sand tray beneath slotted masses; long thin test wire and identical reference wire.
Level 2: Micrometer with ratchet (zero-error checked) at >= 3 orthogonal pairs for d -> A = πd²/4; ruler for L; initial straightening load + Vernier extension readings.
Level 3: Repeat readings during unloading to confirm elastic limit, plot F vs e (straight line through origin), compute E = L × gradient / A.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a concert-hall microphone-array boom of total length L = 4.4 m and mass 14 kg hangs horizontally in equilibrium from two light vertical ceiling wires attached at A and B, separated by 3.5 m. Its centre of gravity G lies 1.12 m to the right of attachment A and 2.38 m to the left of attachment B (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B yield T₁ = 93.39 N ≈ 93.4 N. (b) Force balance gives T₂ = 43.95 N ≈ 43.9 N. (c) wire A carries the greater tension because the centre of gravity is closer to wire A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies moment balance about attachment B.
Applies ΣF_y = 0 to obtain T₂.
Identifies the wire closer to G as carrying greater tension.
Justifies using equal opposite moments about G with shorter lever arm.

items.stem: As shown in the diagram, a harbour lantern mounting boom is a uniform horizontal rod of length L = 1.8 m and mass 5 kg smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at O. A rectangular sign of mass 6.5 kg hangs so that its centre of gravity acts 1.5 m from O. A taut support wire joins the outer end of the rod to the wall at an angle of 44° above the horizontal rod (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the tension T in the angled support wire?
items.workedSolution: Taking moments about hinge O: T sin 44° × 1.8 = (5 × 0.9 + 6.5 × 1.5) × 9.81 = 139.8 N m. Hence T sin 44° = 77.66 N and T = 111.8 N ≈ 112 N. Horizontal balance: R_x = T cos 44° = 80.42 N ≈ 80.4 N. Vertical balance: R_y = (5 + 6.5) × 9.81 − 77.66 = 35.15 N ≈ 35.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 112 N.

items.stem: In Searle's Young modulus investigation (RP4) on a nichrome alloy wire of unstretched length $(2.60 \pm 0.002)$ m, micrometer diameter measurements at three orthogonal positions average to 0.34 mm, 0.32 mm, and 0.33 mm (each $\pm 0.01$ mm). Plotting load $F$ against extension $e$ yields a straight line through the origin of gradient 6.9 N mm⁻¹ ($\pm 1.6\%$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $A = \pi d^2/4 = 8.55 × 10⁻⁸ m²$. (b) $E = L(\mathrm{grad})/A = 210 GPa$. (c) $\%\Delta E = 7.74%$. (d) an identical reference wire compensates both ceiling sag and thermal expansion while orthogonal micrometer diameter measurements reduce cross sectional area uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Averages three diameters and converts mm to m in $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Cross-sectional area $A = 8.55 × 10⁻⁸ m²$.
Converts gradient to N m⁻¹ and substitutes into $E = (L/A)\,\mathrm{grad}$.
Young modulus $E = 210 GPa$.
Combines $\%\Delta L + 2\%\Delta d + \%\Delta\mathrm{grad}$.
Percentage uncertainty in $E = 7.74%$.
Identical reference wire compensates both support sag and temperature expansion.
Orthogonal micrometer readings at >= 3 positions detect non-uniformity/oval cross-section.

items.stem: Under what exact physical condition is the total angular momentum of a multi-disc clutch assembly conserved during engagement?
items.workedSolution: Internal friction torques act equally and oppositely on the two plates, so total angular momentum is conserved provided no resultant external torque acts on the system.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that no resultant external torque acts on the system.

items.stem: An engineering team is redesigning a heavy cast-iron KERS flywheel for a racing prototype to increase energy stored per kilogram while keeping losses low during coasting.
items.workedSolution: From $E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$, concentrating mass at the rim raises $I$, while high-tensile, low-density composites resist bursting stress so $\omega_{\max}$ increases dramatically. An evacuated casing and magnetic bearings minimise windage and friction losses while high-strength rim permits greater angular speed, supported by containment shielding for safety.

markScheme.criterion: States that stored energy $E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ grows linearly with $I$ and quadratically with $\omega$.
Explains that concentrating mass in an outer rim maximises $I = \sum m r^2$ for a given mass.
Explains that centripetal stress limits $\omega_{\max}$ and motivates high tensile strength, low-density composite fibres.
Explains that enclosing the rotor in a vacuum (evacuated casing) drastically reduces aerodynamic windage losses.
Explains that magnetic bearings eliminate solid-on-solid axle contact friction at high angular speeds.
Discusses a safety or operational implication such as an armoured containment casing or gyroscopic torque during vehicle turns.

parts.prompt: Explain the key material, geometric, and housing modifications required to maximise the energy stored safely in a KERS flywheel and minimise parasitic energy losses.
parts.expectedAnswer: Maximum kinetic energy stored depends on half times moment of inertia times angular speed squared, so concentrating mass near the outer rim increases moment of inertia for a given mass while using a low-density, high-tensile-strength carbon-fibre composite prevents the rim from bursting under high centripetal hoop stress at large angular speed. Furthermore, an evacuated casing and magnetic bearings minimise windage and friction losses while high-strength rim permits greater angular speed, and a reinforced containment shroud protects the vehicle if catastrophic failure ever occurs.
workingSteps: L1: State $E_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ and note that energy rises with both $I$ and the square of $\omega$.
L1: Explain that placing mass at the outer rim increases $I = \sum m r^2$ for a fixed mass.
L2: Explain that at high $\omega$, large centripetal forces produce high tensile hoop stress in the rim.
L2: Justify replacing cast iron with high-tensile-strength, low-density composite material to raise safe $\omega_{\max}$.
L3: Explain using an evacuated housing to eliminate aerodynamic windage drag and magnetic bearings to eliminate mechanical axle friction.
L3: Mention safety containment or gyroscopic stability considerations during cornering.

items.stem: In a frictionless pivot stand, a calibration swing mass of mass 2.4 kg on a light string of length 2.3 m is released from rest with the string horizontal and coalesces at the lowest point with stationary a coupling receiver ball of mass 6 kg. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What maximum vertical height above the lowest point do the joined bodies reach?
items.workedSolution: Pre-impact speed u = √(2gL) = 6.71 m s⁻¹. Tangential momentum conservation gives v = mu / (m + M) = 1.92 m s⁻¹. Post-impact rise h = v² / (2g) = (m/(m+M))² L = 0.188 m; energy lost = mgL − (m+M)gh = 38.6 J. Target = 0.188 m.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves energy during swings and momentum during impact to obtain 0.188 m (A).

items.stem: A variable driving torque $T$ acts on a lathe spindle as it turns through an angular displacement $\theta$. What physical quantity is represented by the area enclosed beneath the graph of torque $T$ against angular displacement $\theta$?
items.workedSolution: By rotational analogy with $W = Fs$, incremental work is $\Delta W = T\Delta\theta$, so the area under a torque against angular displacement graph equals work done.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that area under a torque against angular displacement graph equals work done.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a bridge-tower maintenance access gate of length L = 1.8 m and mass 24 kg is smoothly hinged at O to a vertical wall and held horizontally in static equilibrium. Because of an internal reinforcing frame, its centre of gravity G lies 0.83 m from hinge O. A single steel cable attached to the outer edge pulls upward and toward the wall at an angle of 42° to the vertical (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 146.1 N ≈ 146 N. (b) the angled wire exerts a horizontal component pulling toward the wall so the hinge must provide an equal horizontal force away from the wall for translational equilibrium. (c)(i) R_x = 97.75 N, R_y = 126.9 N, so R = 160.2 N ≈ 160 N. (c)(ii) α = tan⁻¹(R_y / R_x) = 52.39° ≈ 52.4° above the horizontal.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Στ = 0 about O using T cos(angle to vertical) × L = m g x_G.
Obtains T = 146.1 N (146 N) matching 1.5e+2 N.
Identifies horizontal component of angled cable tension directed toward the wall.
States hinge must exert an equal opposite horizontal force away from the wall for ΣF_x = 0.
Computes R_x = 97.75 N and R_y = 126.9 N and applies Pythagoras.
Resultant hinge reaction magnitude R = 160 N.
Uses tan α = R_y / R_x with both hinge components.
Direction α = 52.4° above the horizontal.

items.stem: Released from rest at the anchor of an elastic shock cord (natural length 1.8 m) in a high-platform test rig, a bridge-jump test sandbag of mass 9 kg falls freely to point A where the cord becomes taut, then stretches the cord by 1.1 m over 0.12 s before reaching instantaneous rest at B. Assume gravitational field strength g = 9.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_A = √(2gL).
Obtains 5.94 m s⁻¹.
Applies (F_mean − mg)Δt = m v_A, including weight mg.
Mean resultant upward force = (9 × 5.94) / 0.12 = 445 N.
Obtains 534 N.
Uses mg(L + x) = ½kx² and T_B = kx.
Obtains 465 N.

items.stem: In a dry-test tower, a marine mooring weight of mass 7 kg is released from rest at the anchor of a stretchable nylon hawser of unstretched length 2 m. The cord becomes taut at A and stretches obeying Hooke's law by a maximum extension of 0.85 m over 0.34 s before a marine mooring weight comes momentarily to rest at B. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the spring constant of a stretchable nylon hawser?
items.workedSolution: Total vertical drop from release S to lowest point B is L + x = 2 + 0.85 = 2.85 m. By energy conservation mg(L + x) = ½kx², giving k = 2mg(L + x)/x² = 542 N m⁻¹ and peak tension T_B = kx = 460 N. Target = 542 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses full vertical drop (2 + 0.85) m in mg(L + x) = ½kx² to obtain 542 N m⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: The horizontal boom of a marine dry-dock hull gantry crane has total length L = 22 m and mass 400 kg, supported on a vertical mast pivot P located 6 m from the rear end A. A concrete counterweight of mass 4400 kg sits 4.8 m to the left of P (1.2 m from A). The centre of gravity G of the boom itself lies 3 m to the right of P (9 m from A), and the hoist hook hangs 15 m to the right of P (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) M_cw = 2.072 × 10⁵ N m ≈ 2.07 × 10⁵ N m. (b) Equating clockwise and anticlockwise moments about P gives m_max = 1328 kg ≈ 1.33e+3 kg. (c) Vertical force balance yields R = 6.012 × 10⁴ N ≈ 6.01 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses M = m g d with counterweight mass and lever arm from P.
Counterweight moment = 2.07 × 10⁵ N m.
Subtracts boom self-weight moment from counterweight moment and divides by g × load lever arm.
Maximum safe load mass = 1.33e+3 kg.
Applies vertical force balance summing counterweight, boom, and load weights.
Upward mast reaction R = 6.01 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, glider X of mass 5.2 kg moves right at 12 m s⁻¹ and collides with stationary glider Y of mass 1.6 kg. Immediately after impact, glider Y moves right at 10.92 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of glider X immediately after the collision?
items.workedSolution: Momentum conservation: (5.2)(12) = (5.2)v_X + (1.6)(10.92), giving v_X = 8.64 m s⁻¹. K_i = 374 J and K_f = 289 J, so ΔK_lost = K_i − K_f = 84.9 J. Target = 8.64 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Conserves linear momentum and evaluates kinetic energy budget to obtain 8.64 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: On a level low-friction dynamics rail, lighter cart X of mass 1.6 kg moving right at 6 m s⁻¹ strikes stationary heavier cart Y of mass 4.5 kg, causing cart Y to move right at 2.59 m s⁻¹ while cart X rebounds to the left. How much kinetic energy is dissipated in this rebound collision?
items.workedSolution: Taking rightward positive, (1.6)(6) = (1.6)v_X + (4.5)(2.59) gives v_X = -1.28 m s⁻¹ (1.28 m s⁻¹ to the left). Scalar final kinetic energies add: K_f = ½(1.6)(1.28)² + ½(4.5)(2.59)² = 16.4 J. Energy lost = 28.8 J − K_f = 12.4 J. Target = 12.4 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds rebound speed 1.28 m s⁻¹ and sums scalar kinetic energies to obtain 12.4 J (B).

items.stem: In a lecture-hall whirl rig, a calibration ball of mass 1.3 kg whirls in a vertical circle of radius 0.5 m on a thin braided string and passes through the lowest point at speed 4.5 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the tension in a thin braided string at the lowest point?
items.workedSolution: At the bottom, upward resultant force T − mg = mv²/r. Centripetal force mv²/r = 1.3 × 4.5² / 0.5 = 52.6 N, so T = 52.6 + 1.3 × 9.81 = 65.4 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies T = m(v²/r + g) at the bottom of the circle to obtain 65.4 N (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts weight mg instead of adding mg, confusing the bottom of a vertical circle with the top.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates tension directly to centripetal force mv²/r and forgets the downward weight mg.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Sets tension equal to static weight mg, ignoring centripetal acceleration.

items.stem: Launched from a tee on flat ground across a level driving range, a golf launch-monitor ball has an initial speed of 21 m s⁻¹ at 55° above the horizontal. Assume gravitational field strength g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) v_apex = 21 × cos 55°. Answer: 12.0 m s⁻¹. (b) u_y = 21 × sin 55° = 17.2 m s⁻¹. h_max = u_y² / (2 × 9.8). Answer: 15.1 m. (c) T = 2u_y / 9.8 = 3.51 s. R = 12.0 × T. Answer: 42.3 m.

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes v_y = 0 at apex so v_apex = u cos θ.
Obtains 12.0 m s⁻¹.
Applies h_max = (u sin θ)² / (2g).
Obtains 15.1 m.
Evaluates R = u_x × (2u_y / g).
Obtains 42.3 m.

items.stem: In a workshop statics test, a warehouse loading-bay balancing spar AB of length L = 5 m and mass 12 kg has its centre of gravity G at 2.5 m from end A. It is balanced horizontally on a knife-edge pivot P located 1.5 m from end A by placing a 14 kg calibration block to the left of P (use g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) The moment of a force is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. (b) Moment balance about P gives d = 0.8571 m left of P, so distance from end B is 4.357 m ≈ 4.36 m.

markScheme.criterion: Force multiplied by distance from pivot.
Perpendicular distance to the line of action.
Correct moment balance about P yielding lever arm d = 0.8571 m.
Converts cleanly to distance from end B = 4.36 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the distance from end B at which the calibration block must be placed so that the beam balances horizontally.
workingSteps: Clockwise moment of beam weight about P = 12 × 9.81 × 1.000.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, glider X of mass 4 kg moves to the right at 10 m s⁻¹ and collides head-on with glider Y of mass 3.6 kg moving to the left at 4 m s⁻¹ (arrow on Y not shown). Immediately after impact, glider Y moves to the right at 5 m s⁻¹. Take motion to the right as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) p_before = 4 × 10 + 3.6 × (−4) = 25.6 kg m s⁻¹. Answer: 25.6 kg m s⁻¹ to the right. (b) v_X = (25.6 − 3.6 × 5) / 4 = 1.90 m s⁻¹. Answer: 1.90 m s⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_X u_X − m_Y |u_Y| with correct signs.
Obtains 25.6 kg m s⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: As shown in the figure, a surveyor's creek-crossing timber plank of total length L = 6.8 m and mass 40 kg rests horizontally on two narrow supports A and B. Support A is positioned at its left end, and support B is 4.6 m to the right of A, leaving an unsupported right-hand overhang of 2.2 m. A technician of mass 86 kg initially stands 2.7 m from the left end of the plank (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Moments about B give F₁ = 450.8 N ≈ 451 N. (b) Vertical equilibrium gives F₂ = 785.2 N ≈ 785 N. (c) the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases. (d) Setting F₁ = 0 about B yields d_tip = 0.5581 m ≈ 0.558 m.

markScheme.criterion: Takes moments about B summing plank and technician anticlockwise moments.
Support A reaction F₁ = 451 N.
Support B reaction F₂ = 785 N via vertical force balance.
States that the reaction force at support A decreases and the reaction force at support B increases.
Sets F₁ = 0 and equates clockwise overhang moment to restoring plank moment about B.
Tipping distance past B = 0.558 m.
